translations.answer: The original Isaac Gym uses average, while the Isaac Lab locomotion example uses multiply. An example is given: when foot friction is 1 and ground friction is 0, average yields 0.5, while multiply yields 0. Therefore, directly transferring friction parameters would alter the equivalent contact friction. This explanation clarifies the parameter semantics, but does not prove it to be the sole cause of Go2 failure.
translations.applicability: Applies to friction parameter migration from Isaac Gym/legged-gym to Isaac Lab locomotion environment.
translations.credibility.rationale: Environmental, processing steps, and results have engineering records, but formal cross-validation or independent replication is lacking.
translations.details.attempts.0: The questioner randomized static friction to 0.8–2.0 and dynamic friction to 0.6–1.6.
translations.details.attempts.1: The contributor explains the difference between Isaac Gym's average and Isaac Lab locomotion's multiply.
translations.details.attempts.2: Go1 users reported using a wider friction range, actuator-net, a physics/policy frequency ratio of about 10 times, and specific foot-end rewards.
translations.details.diagnostics.1: Check foot-end contact sensor and air-time reward.
translations.details.diagnostics.2: Compare friction randomization range, reward terms, actuator model, and policy/physics dt.
translations.details.environments.0: Isaac Lab locomotion; Unitree Go2 question environment; community Go1/ANYmal-D experience; specific Isaac Lab commit not mentioned.
translations.details.limits.0: Mix Go2, Go1, and ANYmal-D in threads; numerical values cannot be directly transposed across robots.
translations.details.limits.1: Community users explicitly stated some suggestions are based on personal testing or not yet tested; the post lacks a unified closed-loop.
translations.details.outcomes.0: The questioner reported that friction randomization helped significantly and achieved initial Go2 Sim-to-Real, but still tends to fall.
translations.details.outcomes.1: Go1 users reported good migration and less foot slippage, but no independent replication.
translations.details.problem_statements.0: The simulation strategy relies on dragging the foot, but fails to move when deployed on Go2.
translations.details.problem_statements.1: Foot friction randomization allows initial migration, but gait remains unnatural and prone to falling.
translations.details.suspected_causes.0: The friction combination mode in simulation differs from the assets and rewards that make dragging the foot a usable behavior.
translations.details.suspected_causes.1: The actuator model does not match real-world dynamics.
translations.details.symptoms.0: The simulated foot does not lift, dragging the ground.
translations.details.symptoms.1: The real-world strategy cannot move or easily falls.
translations.details.symptoms.2: Friction randomization leads to pronking-like gait.
translations.source.title: Friction, rewards, and actuator experience cause Sim-to-Real failure in Go2 due to foot dragging
